I used to order takeout three nights a week.
Every Friday I would swing by the bakery on the way home.
I used to live within walking distance of everything.
In 2021 I moved to the countryside.
So you were in Sao Paulo for forty years. What did you do every single day there that you do not do now?
Takeout. I used to order takeout three nights a week, and I did not even look at the menu.
Because cooking after work was a hassle.
Exactly. And nothing here is within walking distance, so now I cook. I did not use to cook at all.
I had the same thing with the shop. In Oslo I would stop there on the way home every evening. Now I stock up once a week and I plan it.
That is the part nobody warns you about. An errand used to take ten minutes. Now it takes an afternoon.
And do you miss it, or do you only miss the convenience?
Neither, really. I miss being a creature of habit without organizing it. Even winding down is something I schedule now.
I did not use to cook at all, and now I cook every night.
It was second nature. I never decided to do it.
An errand used to take ten minutes. Now it takes an afternoon.

My name is Lars. I lived in Oslo for eighteen years and I moved out four years ago, and people always ask me what I miss. For a long time I said nothing, and that was not honest. What I miss is small. I used to walk down to the same coffee place every morning before seven, and the man there did not ask me what I wanted, he just started making it. That was second nature. I did not choose it. On Fridays my brother and I would meet at the station and take the last train together, and we never planned it once. Now I stock up on Saturday, I drive everywhere, and an errand takes half a day. Is it better? Yes. Do I miss the coffee man? Also yes. Both things are true, and nobody ever tells you that before you move.

I am Ruth, and I went the other way round. I grew up in a village in Yorkshire and I moved to London at twenty-six, and everybody expected me to talk about the traffic. What I actually noticed was the loss of the boring parts. At home I used to leave the house without locking the door, and I did not think about it, ever. Every Sunday my father and I would drive to the reservoir and say almost nothing for an hour. In London nothing is mundane in that way. Everything is a small decision, all day long. I do not want to go back, and I am not being sentimental. I am only saying that what I dreaded about moving was the noise, and what I actually lost was the part of the day where I was not deciding anything.
